intro.text: I benchmark GPU kernels and write up what the measurements actually show. The posts here are experiments on real hardware, including NVIDIA L4 and T4 and AMD MI300X, down to the PTX, SASS, and hardware-counter level.

posts.title: Attention kernels on MI300X: a utilization story
posts.description: Benchmarking FlashAttention kernels on AMD MI300X — AITER vs Triton vs PyTorch SDPA, with hardware counters explaining the throughput ranking. 60 data points, 3 figures.

figures.caption: Throughput across the shape grid. Three implementations, five sequence lengths, two head dimensions. AITER leads at every cell; SDPA tracks the Triton baseline closely.
figures.alt: Attention forward-pass throughput vs sequence length on MI300X, faceted by head dimension

figures.caption: Matrix-core utilization across the same grid. AITER's 72% at head_dim=128, N=16384 sits more than twice as high as the Triton-lineage kernels' 33–34% plateau.
figures.alt: MFMA matrix-core utilization vs sequence length on MI300X, faceted by head dimension

figures.caption: Throughput plotted against MFMA utilization for every (implementation, shape) cell. Points fall along a single rising band: high utilization means high throughput, across implementations and across shapes.

posts.title: Safe Rust on the GPU, at the PTX level: what cuda-oxide actually emits
posts.description: A PTX/SASS-level comparison of cuda-oxide (safe Rust to PTX) against clang and nvcc on three GPU kernels — where the overhead comes from, whether it amortizes, and what it costs at runtime on an L4. 3 figures.

figures.caption: The three compile paths. cuda-oxide and clang share the upstream LLVM 21 backend, so comparing them isolates the language; clang and nvcc share the language but differ in the backend.
figures.alt: Three compile paths: cuda-oxide, clang, and nvcc, and the backends they share

figures.caption: PTX instruction count per kernel. cuda-oxide is ~2.5x on the tiny kernels but reaches parity with nvcc on the reduction, where the kernel's own work dominates the fixed prologue.
figures.alt: PTX instruction count per kernel for cuda-oxide, clang, and nvcc

figures.caption: cuda-oxide relative to nvcc. The 2.46x static PTX overhead on vecadd and gather costs essentially nothing at runtime; the only measurable cost is the reduction's few percent, where the PTX is already at parity.
figures.alt: cuda-oxide relative to nvcc: large static PTX overhead, near-zero runtime cost

posts.title: Language or backend? Adding rust-cuda to my GPU code comparison
posts.description: A 2×2 follow-up that adds rust-cuda (Rust → libNVVM) to the cuda-oxide study, so language and backend can be separated. The two Rust compilers turn out to make opposite safety choices; the compute-bound speed gap is real but not a pure backend effect. 3 figures.

figures.caption: The four compilers as a 2×2. Each column shares a backend; each row shares a language. cuda-oxide is highlighted because it is the only cell that uses generic addressing — a behavior not shared by the other Rust compiler or the other upstream-LLVM compiler.
figures.alt: The 2x2 grid: Rust and C++ rows, upstream LLVM and libNVVM columns, with the four compilers cuda-oxide, rust-cuda, clang, nvcc

figures.caption: gather is the kernel with the largest difference in the emitted code: cuda-oxide emits about 2.5× the instructions of the C++ compilers, and rust-cuda adds two bounds-check traps for the data-dependent read. Yet at runtime all four were equal within measurement noise (about 5694 µs), because this kernel waits on memory.
figures.alt: Bar chart of PTX instruction counts for gather: oxide 64, rustcuda 36, clang 25, nvcc 26

figures.caption: reduction median time per launch (locked clock, 50 rounds × 200 reps). The two C++ compilers are a little faster than the two Rust compilers. Note: the axis starts at 320 µs to make the small gap visible. The cause is not established, and it is not a pure backend effect — if it were, the two libNVVM tools (nvcc and rust-cuda) would group together, and they do not.
figures.alt: Bar chart of reduction median microseconds per launch: nvcc 337, clang 344, oxide 351, rustcuda 354

posts.title: Found it: the Rust GPU speed gap was a 64-bit loop counter
posts.description: Follow-up to the 2×2 study, which left a ~3–5% Rust deficit on the reduction kernel as "cause not established". Reading the SASS pointed at 64-bit (usize) loop indexing; a three-line u32 change removes the gap completely. 3 figures.

figures.caption: One round of the tree loop, instruction by instruction. The three extras in rust-cuda (orange) are the upper halves of 64-bit operations: a compare, a shift, and the loop test. The listing is simplified for readability; order and pairing follow the committed SASS.
figures.alt: The reduction tree loop instruction by instruction: nvcc 10 instructions, rust-cuda 13, with the three extras highlighted as upper halves of 64-bit operations

figures.caption: Whole-kernel SASS instruction counts. The C++ versions are unchanged between the two groups; only the Rust loop index changed. After the change: exact parity, 48 across the board.
figures.alt: SASS instruction totals before and after: 48/48/56/56 becomes 48/48/48/48

figures.caption: Median time per launch, before and after. Note: the axis starts at 310 µs to make the small gap visible. Before the change, both Rust versions are last; after it, both are first — within the run-to-run noise of nvcc, so the honest statement is "the gap is gone", not "Rust is now faster".
figures.alt: Runtime bars before and after: Rust versions go from last to first

posts.title: Benchmarking a moving target: my cuda-oxide results changed in weeks
posts.description: A follow-up to my cuda-oxide study. Re-testing weeks later, two of three findings had changed — and one change dropped a safe-indexing bounds check, so safe Rust code reads out of bounds (confirmed by compute-sanitizer, reported as cuda-oxide #396). Also: why the version tag does not pin the compiler. 3 figures.

figures.caption: The front part is version-tagged, but it downloads the back part from the latest branch. So two version tags can give you the same backend — or different ones on different days.
figures.alt: Two version tags both fetch the same backend commit from the latest branch

figures.caption: Older build vs newer build across the three kernels. Addressing improved everywhere; size is mixed; the gather bounds check was dropped.
figures.alt: Table: addressing improved on all three kernels; size mixed; gather bounds check dropped

figures.caption: The same safe-Rust program with one out-of-range index. The older build guards the access (0 errors); the newer build reads ~4 MB out of bounds (invalid read). Reported as issue #396.
figures.alt: Same program: older build 0 errors, newer build invalid out-of-bounds read

posts.title: How close to peak is a simple softmax? Two GPUs, one measurement trap
posts.description: Softmax is memory-bound, so the question is simple: what fraction of bandwidth does it reach? I tested three optimizations on an L4 and an MI300X; the data rejected all three. The reason was more interesting than a speedup — most of my measurements were reading cache, not memory, and one GPU showed a mirage the other could not. On measuring your real ceiling, spotting cache-resident benchmarks, and knowing when an operation simply cannot fill the GPU. 3 figures.

figures.caption: Spec-sheet bandwidth against what a plain copy actually reaches, on both GPUs.
figures.alt: Spec-sheet bandwidth against what a plain copy actually reaches, on both GPUs.

figures.caption: Percentage of measured peak bandwidth against tensor size. In the shaded region the data fits in cache, so the numbers describe the cache and can pass 100%. Once the data spills cache, the two kernels agree.
figures.alt: Percentage of measured peak bandwidth against tensor size. In the shaded region the data fits in cache, so the numbers describe the cache and can pass 100%. Once the data spills cache, the two kernels agree.

figures.caption: The same simple kernel on both GPUs. Past each dotted line the data no longer fits that GPU's cache. The L4 reaches its limit; the MI300X flattens at about half of its own.
figures.alt: The same simple kernel on both GPUs. Past each dotted line the data no longer fits that GPU's cache. The L4 reaches its limit; the MI300X flattens at about half of its own.

posts.title: A cliff below the cache: why a softmax slows down before it should
posts.description: A follow-up to the softmax study. On the L4, the bandwidth cliff arrives at ~27 MB, below the 48 MB cache. Why? I guessed multi-pass reuse and was wrong: re-reading one small row costs almost no extra time (confirmed in the PTX). The real cause is that input and output share the cache, so a read-only kernel cliffs at ~55 MB, almost exactly double. 2 figures.

figures.caption: The cache as a fixed box. Read-write must hold input and output together, so input can only reach about half the cache before it overflows. Read-only holds input alone, so input can reach the whole cache — and the cliff moves to twice the size.
figures.alt: The cache as a fixed box. Read-write must hold input and output together, so input can only reach about half the cache before it overflows. Read-only holds input alone, so input can reach the whole cache — and the cliff moves to twice the size.

figures.caption: Input bandwidth as a percentage of measured peak, against input size. The read-write kernel cliffs at about 27 MB; the read-only kernel stays fast until about 55 MB — almost exactly double, because removing the output frees half the cache.
figures.alt: Input bandwidth as a percentage of measured peak, against input size. The read-write kernel cliffs at about 27 MB; the read-only kernel stays fast until about 55 MB — almost exactly double, because removing the output frees half the cache.

posts.title: FP8 on Ada with cuda-oxide, checked on real silicon
posts.description: cuda-oxide lets you write GPU kernels in Rust. Its FP8 support for Ada (sm_89) was largely auto-generated, so I checked it on a real L4: FP8 conversions and the full m16n8k16 tensor-core MMA family, verified numerically correct against CPU references, with clean PTX. Generated is not the same as verified, so this fills in that gap. 1 figure.

figures.caption: A simplified picture of the idea: the matrix is split across all 32 threads of a group, each holding specific cells. The real pattern is more intricate, but the point is the same: every piece must land in exactly the right place, or the result is wrong.
